claims.text: The as-built additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has an FCC matrix.
The starting material exhibits minimal oxidation and secondary-phase formation.
Exposure to oxidizing gas at 700–1000 °C produces multicomponent oxide scales.
An appreciable oxygen partial pressure causes rapid or excessive oxide-scale growth.
Oxide scales form and spall preferentially at grain boundaries.
Oxide formation causes localized depletion of Cr and Ti from grain-boundary regions of the matrix.
Cr- and Ti-depleted interfaces destabilize and embrittle the FCC matrix.
Embrittled, oxide-affected interfaces initiate microcracking that can progress to catastrophic fracture.
A reducing, H2-rich environment suppresses oxide-scale growth.
Suppressing oxide growth in reducing gas limits local elemental depletion, preserves ductility, and delays catastrophic fracture.
Relative to an inert baseline, strongly oxidizing exposure produces a thicker oxide layer.
Relative to an inert baseline, strongly oxidizing exposure increases grain-boundary cracking and reduces fracture toughness.
Inert or near-inert exposure produces minimal mass gain and preserves mechanical integrity.
The proposed oxidation-controlled mechanism applies throughout 700–1000 °C in O2/H2 environments.
At temperatures or partial pressures outside the proposed range, internal nitridation could become the dominant degradation mechanism.
Under highly reducing conditions, secondary phases such as nitrides might form and contribute to embrittlement.
Systematically varying O2/H2 partial pressures while measuring mass change, oxide structure, and mechanical properties is the proposed controlled test.
The hypothesis is falsified if gas partial pressure does not alter oxide scales or failure modes, or if mechanical degradation does not track oxide formation.
